definition: Generative topographic map (GTM) is a machine learning method that is a probabilistic counterpart of the self-organizing map (SOM), is probably convergent and does not require a shrinking neighborhood or a decreasing step size.
details: It is a generative model: the data is assumed to arise by first probabilistically picking a point in a low-dimensional space, mapping the point to the observed high-dimensional input space (via a smooth function), then adding noise in that space. The parameters of the low-dimensional probability distribution, the smooth map and the noise are all learned from the training data using the expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm. GTM was introduced in 1996 in a paper by Christopher Bishop, Markus Svensen, and Christopher K. I. Williams.

explainer.lead: A generative topographic map, or GTM, learns a smooth, low-dimensional description of complex data while also modelling uncertainty. It offers a probabilistic alternative to the self-organizing map, with parameters learned directly from training data.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a bendy sheet hidden inside a cloud of dots: each dot starts as a point on the sheet, is stretched into its final position, and then gets a small random nudge. GTM learns the sheet's shape and how big those nudges usually are. This lets it explain complicated data using just a few hidden coordinates.
tiers.practitioner: Use GTM when data is plausibly generated by a smooth low-dimensional manifold plus noise. Fit the latent distribution, mapping, and noise parameters with the EM algorithm rather than applying SOM-style neighbourhood and step-size schedules. Its usefulness depends on those generative assumptions fitting the data.
tiers.paperLevel: A GTM defines x in a low-dimensional latent space, maps it smoothly as f(x; theta) into the observed space, and generates an observation z = f(x; theta) + epsilon, where epsilon is noise. The latent distribution, f, and the noise parameters are estimated from training data by expectation–maximization. Introduced by Christopher Bishop, Markus Svensen, and Christopher K. I. Williams in 1996, it is a probabilistic counterpart of the SOM that does not require a shrinking neighbourhood or decreasing step size.

explainer.example: Suppose each observation is a vector of 100 measurements, but the measurements mostly vary with two underlying factors. GTM can represent those factors as a two-dimensional latent point, learn a smooth mapping from that point into the 100-dimensional space, and model the remaining measurement variation as noise.
explainer.intuition: Complex observations can often be pictured as noisy points around a curved, low-dimensional surface. GTM turns that picture into a generative model: choose a latent point, smoothly map it into the observation space, then add noise.
howItWorks: Choose a low-dimensional latent space with a probability distribution over its points.
Draw a latent point from that distribution.
Pass the point through a learned smooth function to obtain a position in the high-dimensional observation space.
Add noise to produce an observation.
Use the EM algorithm on training data to learn the latent distribution, smooth map, and noise parameters.
explainer.whyItMatters: GTM combines dimensionality reduction with an explicit account of how observations and their noise are generated. Its probabilistic training procedure also avoids the shrinking neighbourhood and decreasing step size required by a self-organizing map.
misconceptions: It is not simply a self-organizing map with a different training schedule; it is a probabilistic generative model.
Its smooth map goes from the low-dimensional latent space to the high-dimensional observation space, not the other way around.
The latent coordinates do not reproduce observations exactly because the model also includes noise.
